title: Mouse control matters more than memorized distance
summary: Changing sensitivity or peripherals does not erase aim skill. Strong aim comes from adaptable hand-eye coordination and fine motor control, not preserving one exact force-distance memory forever.
why: Even on one constant sensitivity, pad wear, skates, humidity, and friction change the force needed from day to day.
If aiming really depended on memorizing one exact force for one exact distance, consistent high-level aim would already be impossible under normal setup variance.
actions: Treat sensitivity as an adjustable tool rather than proof of identity or progress.
When testing a new setup, judge crosshair control after a short reacclimation period instead of panicking over the first few minutes.
Use skill transfer and control quality as the standard, not whether the new setup feels identical instantly.
avoid: Do not assume every setup change destroys progress.
Avoid using the muscle-memory myth as the default explanation for every slump.

evidence.claim: Aiming skill is better explained by adaptable mouse control and hand-eye coordination than by memorizing one exact sensitivity distance relationship.
evidence.excerpt: Good aim is about developing the motor control to move the crosshair where you want it even with unfamiliar settings or peripherals.
